Previously a value of 1.4 has been adopted, as used in P+20 and B+20. We show in the inset panel that this is approximately where only one single star in a million is removed from DR2. sites.window: sing the UWE/RUWE The calculation of Unit Weight Error (UWE) requires normalising the residuals between observations and a single source model using the astrometric error, sigma _ ast . This is not a known quantity, depending at the very least on the colour and apparent magnitude ( m_G ) of the source, which affects the performance of the telescopes' CCDs. Incorrectly estimating sigma _ ast will cause the peak in UWE of a population dominated by single stars to stray from the expected value of 1. Phrased another way, the modal UWE of a population of well behaved sources of a particular magnitude and colour can be used to infer the true astrometric error, showing us (if we could identify a truly well-behaved population) how to rescale whatever error was previously assumed. Here, we exploit the exquisite astrometric precision of Gaia to carry out the largest to date comparative study into the binarity of matched samples of nearby B and Be stars from the Bright Star Catalogue. To aid in accounting for these complications, we considered additional information that might hint at, or in some cases confirm, the binary nature of an object. This included the Renormalized Unit Weight Error (RUWE) from Gaia <<CITE:Lindegren:2018>> , which is a measure of the quality of the astrometric solution. RUWE values in excess of 1.4 can often be a sign of unmodeled binary motion. For each object, we also checked the \tt ipd_frac_multi_peak parameter from the Gaia DR3 catalog, which indicates the fraction of the time the object appeared to have more than one peak in scans oriented in different directions. Because the binary fraction of metal-poor stars is high <<CITE:moe19>> , we next check ExoFOP <<FN>> and the Gaia DR3 catalog <<CITE:gaiadr3vallenari>> for evidence of binarity. We discard targets for which speckle or adaptive optics imaging has revealed a close companion. For stars lacking such high-resolution follow-up imaging, close neighbors in the Gaia stellar catalog, a high reduced unit weight error <<CITE:belokurov20,penoyre22,gaiadr3arenou>> , or an ipd_frac_multi_peak value above 2 <<CITE:gaiaedr3fabricius,gaiaedr3smart,elbadry21>> may indicate binarity. Although a binary companion does not necessarily mean that the TESS signal is of non-planetary origin, it significantly complicates the follow-up, making it challenging to determine which star hosts the transit and potentially biasing precision radial velocity measurements.
